c01.display: Welcome to unit three of NLP, Simply Explained. This is lesson 1: constituency parsing.
c01.spoken: Welcome to unit three of N L P, Simply Explained. This is lesson 1: constituency parsing.

c02.display: In unit two we tagged words and grouped them into small chunks. Now we go all the way, and find the complete structure of a sentence.
c02.spoken: In unit two we tagged words and grouped them into small chunks. Now we go all the way, and find the complete structure of a sentence.

c03.display: Here's the idea. A sentence isn't a flat list of words. It's a tree: phrases nested inside bigger phrases.
c03.spoken: Here's the idea. A sentence isn't a flat list of words. It's a tree: phrases nested inside bigger phrases.

c04.display: The building blocks are called constituents. A constituent is a group of words that works as one unit. A quick test: can you replace the group with a single word?
c04.spoken: The building blocks are called constituents. A constituent is a group of words that works as one unit. A quick test: can you replace the group with a single word?

c05.display: In "the old man slept", you can replace "the old man" with "he". So "the old man" is a constituent.
c05.spoken: In "the old man slept", you can replace "the old man" with "he". So "the old man" is a constituent.

c06.display: Think of nesting boxes. Small boxes are packed inside bigger boxes, and the biggest box holds the whole sentence.
c06.spoken: Think of nesting boxes. Small boxes are packed inside bigger boxes, and the biggest box holds the whole sentence.

c07.display: Let's build the tree for "the old man slept", from the bottom up.
c07.spoken: Let's build the tree for "the old man slept", from the bottom up.

c08.display: Words: we start with the four words at the bottom of the tree.
c08.spoken: Words: we start with the four words at the bottom of the tree.

c09.display: Noun phrase: "the old man" joins into one noun phrase, NP.
c09.spoken: Noun phrase: "the old man" joins into one noun phrase, N P.

c10.display: Verb phrase: "slept" forms the verb phrase, VP.
c10.spoken: Verb phrase: "slept" forms the verb phrase, V P.

c11.display: Sentence: finally, the noun phrase and the verb phrase join into the whole sentence, S, at the top of the tree.
c11.spoken: Sentence: finally, the noun phrase and the verb phrase join into the whole sentence, S, at the top of the tree.

c12.display: A parser knows which joins are allowed from a set of rules, called a context-free grammar. Here's a tiny one.
c12.spoken: A parser knows which joins are allowed from a set of rules, called a context-free grammar. Here's a tiny one.

c13.display: S goes to NP VP: a sentence is a noun phrase followed by a verb phrase.
c13.spoken: S goes to N P V P: a sentence is a noun phrase followed by a verb phrase.

c14.display: NP goes to determiner, adjective, noun: like "the old man".
c14.spoken: N P goes to determiner, adjective, noun: like "the old man".

c15.display: VP goes to VERB NP: a verb followed by its object, like "saw a dog".
c15.spoken: V P goes to VERB N P: a verb followed by its object, like "saw a dog".

c16.display: And VP can also be just a verb on its own, like "slept".
c16.spoken: And V P can also be just a verb on its own, like "slept".

c17.display: Here's why parsing is hard. Take: "I saw the man with the telescope."
c17.spoken: Here's why parsing is hard. Take: "I saw the man with the telescope."

c18.display: In one tree, "with the telescope" belongs to "the man". The man is the one holding the telescope.
c18.spoken: In one tree, "with the telescope" belongs to "the man". The man is the one holding the telescope.

c19.display: In the other tree, it belongs to "saw". I used the telescope to see him. Same words, two different trees.
c19.spoken: In the other tree, it belongs to "saw". I used the telescope to see him. Same words, two different trees.

c20.display: So how does a parser choose between trees? It gives each grammar rule a probability. That's a probabilistic context-free grammar, or PCFG. The probabilities are learned by counting rules in a treebank: a large set of sentences that people have parsed by hand.
c20.spoken: So how does a parser choose between trees? It gives each grammar rule a probability. That's a probabilistic context-free grammar, or P C F G. The probabilities are learned by counting rules in a treebank: a large set of sentences that people have parsed by hand.

c21.display: Common rules, like a verb followed by its object, get high probabilities. Rare rules get low ones. The tree whose rules are most likely overall wins.
c21.spoken: Common rules, like a verb followed by its object, get high probabilities. Rare rules get low ones. The tree whose rules are most likely overall wins.

c22.display: Think of a sat-nav. There are many possible routes, and it picks the one most likely to get you there.
c22.spoken: Think of a sat-nav. There are many possible routes, and it picks the one most likely to get you there.

c23.display: A sentence can have thousands of possible trees, so the parser needs a smart search. A classic one is called CKY. Here's the idea.
c23.spoken: A sentence can have thousands of possible trees, so the parser needs a smart search. A classic one is called C K Y. Here's the idea.

c24.display: First, find the best phrases for every pair of neighbouring words.
c24.spoken: First, find the best phrases for every pair of neighbouring words.

c25.display: Then for every run of three words, then four, and so on.
c25.spoken: Then for every run of three words, then four, and so on.

c26.display: Each bigger step reuses the small results already found, so nothing is worked out twice.
c26.spoken: Each bigger step reuses the small results already found, so nothing is worked out twice.

c27.display: When it reaches the full sentence, the best tree over all the words wins.
c27.spoken: When it reaches the full sentence, the best tree over all the words wins.

c28.display: Quick quiz. Why does "I saw the man with the telescope" have two different trees?
c28.spoken: Quick quiz. Why does "I saw the man with the telescope" have two different trees?

c30.display: Because "with the telescope" can attach to "saw", or to "the man". Each choice gives a different tree, and a different meaning.
c30.spoken: Because "with the telescope" can attach to "saw", or to "the man". Each choice gives a different tree, and a different meaning.

c31.display: Let's recap. A sentence is a tree of phrases inside phrases.
c31.spoken: Let's recap. A sentence is a tree of phrases inside phrases.

c32.display: A context-free grammar lists which joins are allowed.
c32.spoken: A context-free grammar lists which joins are allowed.

c33.display: Many sentences can be parsed into more than one tree.
c33.spoken: Many sentences can be parsed into more than one tree.

c34.display: And a probabilistic grammar, a PCFG, picks the most likely tree.
c34.spoken: And a probabilistic grammar, a P C F G, picks the most likely tree.

c35.spoken: Next lesson: Dependency Parsing. How do words in a sentence depend on each other?
